title: The Taliban made girls’ exclusion government policy. The ICC says that policy may be a crime against humanity.
subtitle: Four arrest warrants now name Afghanistan’s supreme leader, chief justice and the ministers responsible for school and university policy. The decision treats institutional exclusion—not only individual acts of violence—as alleged gender persecution, but no arrest is imminent.
author: ATHENA
body:
ARCHIVE REPORT · Originally reported 6 October 2026.

The International Criminal Court has unsealed arrest warrants for four senior Taliban figures, alleging that they used the institutions of government to persecute women and girls—and people who did not conform to the Taliban’s gender policy—after the group returned to power in Afghanistan.

The warrants name Taliban supreme leader Haibatullah Akhundzada; Abdul Hakim Haqqani, president of the Supreme Court; education minister Habibullah Agha; and higher education minister Neda Mohammad Nadim. The first two warrants were issued on 8 July 2025 and made public at the time. The warrants for the two education ministers were issued on 9 September 2025. All four were unsealed on 5 October 2026. The development is therefore the disclosure of the full set of judicial documents, not four new decisions made this week. International Criminal Court:
https://icccpi-web.icccpi-prod.uniccloud.org/news/icc-pre-trial-chamber-ii-unseals-four-arrest-warrants-situation-afghanistan

ICC judges found “reasonable grounds to believe” that the men were responsible for ordering, inducing or soliciting persecution as a crime against humanity. That is the legal threshold for issuing an arrest warrant, not a verdict. None of the four has been tried or convicted by the court, and the allegations would have to be tested through proceedings in which the accused can challenge the evidence.

The Taliban rejects the court’s position. Spokesperson Zabihullah Mujahid said Afghanistan does not recognise the ICC and attaches no importance to the warrants. Reuters:
https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/icc-issues-arrest-warrants-two-taliban-leaders-2026-10-05/

## Education is part of the alleged crime—not a side issue

The inclusion of the education and higher education ministers matters. It locates responsibility not only in the Taliban’s supreme leadership and courts, but in the departments that turned exclusion into everyday administration.

The ICC says the alleged persecution included severe deprivation of the rights to education, privacy and family life, movement, expression, thought, conscience and religion. Judges connected that policy to alleged acts including murder, imprisonment, torture, rape and enforced disappearance between 15 August 2021 and at least 20 January 2025. International Criminal Court:
https://icccpi-web.icccpi-prod.uniccloud.org/news/icc-pre-trial-chamber-ii-unseals-four-arrest-warrants-situation-afghanistan

This does not mean every restriction is automatically a crime against humanity. Under the Rome Statute, persecution requires the intentional and severe deprivation of fundamental rights because of a group’s identity, in connection with another crime within the court’s jurisdiction or another crime against humanity. The prosecution would still have to prove the elements of the offence and each suspect’s responsibility.

But the warrants reject a narrow idea of persecution as a collection of isolated assaults. The chamber said systemic and institutional harm, discriminatory rules and gendered social expectations may form part of the crime. It interpreted gender as encompassing socially constructed roles and hierarchies, not only biological sex.

That framing reflects the way authoritarian policy reaches private life. A decree can determine whether a girl enters secondary school, whether a woman works, whether she travels without a male relative, and whether a family can afford health care after losing her income. The harm is distributed through ministries, courts, employers and checkpoints—even when there is no single violent incident to place at the centre of every story.

## The case reaches beyond women and girls

The court says the alleged persecution also targeted people perceived as failing to conform to the Taliban’s gender policy, including members of the LGBTQI+ community, and people seen as supporting women and girls. A person did not necessarily have to organise a protest: the chamber said perceived resistance could include passive behaviour or omission.

That breadth is legally and socially important. Gender rule is maintained not only by restricting women, but by punishing people who refuse assigned roles, defend others or live outside the hierarchy. It also means reporting on the case should not erase Afghan men who support women’s rights or gender-diverse people whose exposure may be especially dangerous.

The allegations nevertheless sit within an unequal daily reality. Reuters, citing UN Women, reported that about half of Afghan women leave their homes only once or twice a month and that Afghanistan remains the only country where girls are barred from secondary education and women from universities. These figures describe survey findings and national policy; they do not mean every woman has the same experience or freedom of movement. Reuters:
https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/icc-issues-arrest-warrants-two-taliban-leaders-2026-10-05/

![Official archive portrait of Rosemary DiCarlo](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/dd/Rosemary_DiCarlo_official_portrait.jpg)
Archive portrait: Rosemary DiCarlo, 23 August 2005 (photographic metadata). Photograph: Ann Thomas / US Department of State, via Wikimedia Commons. Public domain US government work. This portrait does not depict her October 2026 Afghanistan visit.
https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Rosemary_DiCarlo_official_portrait.jpg

Afghan women have continued to document restrictions, teach through community programmes and advocate inside and outside the country. On 5 October, UN political affairs chief Rosemary DiCarlo said she had met women leaders, civil society representatives and female UN personnel during a visit to Afghanistan, and had raised girls’ education and restrictions on female staff with the de facto authorities. These meetings show continued agency; they do not establish that the authorities have agreed to reverse the policies. United Nations Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs:
https://dppa.un.org/en/press-releases/note-to-correspondents-under-secretary-general-for-political-and-peacebuilding

## A warrant is not an arrest

The ICC has no police force. It depends on its member states and other cooperating authorities to arrest suspects and transfer them to The Hague. The Taliban leaders remain in Afghanistan, and there is no indication that any of the four is about to enter court custody. ICC cooperation guidance:
https://www.icc-cpi.int/about/cooperation

Afghanistan became a party to the Rome Statute in 2003, which is the basis for the court’s territorial jurisdiction over alleged crimes committed there. The Taliban’s refusal to recognise the court does not by itself remove that jurisdiction; it does make enforcement far more difficult. ICC Afghanistan situation:
https://www.icc-cpi.int/afghanistan

![International Criminal Court headquarters in The Hague in April 2016](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/46/International_Criminal_Court_Headquarters%2C_Netherlands.jpg)
Archive photograph: International Criminal Court headquarters, The Hague, 3 April 2016. Photograph: Hypergio / Wikimedia Commons. CC BY-SA 4.0; original image displayed to fit.
https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:International_Criminal_Court_Headquarters,_Netherlands.jpg
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/

The warrants can still have consequences. If a suspect travels to a cooperating state, the authorities may face a request to arrest him. The documents can also preserve judicial findings, identify lines of command and make it harder for governments to treat the officials solely as conventional diplomatic counterparts.

Those effects should not be overstated. A warrant cannot reopen a school, restore a woman’s job, protect a protester or pay the legal and living costs of an Afghan family in exile. Nor does international attention reliably translate into safe participation for witnesses and survivors.

The practical accountability test now extends beyond whether the ICC has named senior men. States that support the investigation must decide whether they will execute warrants, protect evidence and witnesses, fund Afghan women-led documentation, and avoid diplomatic arrangements that quietly make the warrants irrelevant.

The court’s decision is significant because it recognises a form of power women know intimately: rules can injure at population scale without arriving as a single spectacular act. A school door closed by policy, a job prohibited by decree and a journey conditioned on male permission are not lesser concerns simply because they are bureaucratic.

But legal recognition is not liberation. The measure of this case will be whether it produces cooperation and accountability—and whether Afghan women, girls and gender-diverse people gain greater safety, education and control over their own lives while the proceedings remain unresolved.

The Athena Perspective.
